title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
keyIdea: Sorted → start at both ends. Sum too small: the left number can't reach target with anyone, move left right. Too big: the right number is too big for anyone, move right left. Every step rules out one number for good, so it's one pass with O(1) space.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.why: n·(n−1)/2 pairs: ~4.5·10⁸ at n = 3·10⁴. Ignores the sorting.

approaches.name: Binary search for each partner
approaches.idea: For each i, binary-search the part to its right for target − numbers[i].
approaches.why: n binary searches of O(log n) each. Uses the sorting, but only half as well as two pointers.

approaches.name: Hash map (Two Sum I)
approaches.idea: Same one pass as Two Sum I: look up target − numbers[i], then save numbers[i] → i.
approaches.why: One pass with O(1) map operations, but the map can grow to n entries.
approaches.warn: The problem asks for constant extra space, so this doesn't meet the requirement.

approaches.name: Two pointers
approaches.idea: left = 0, right = n − 1. Sum == target → return {left + 1, right + 1}. Sum < target → left++. Sum > target → right--.
approaches.why: Each step moves one pointer inward, so at most n − 1 steps. Two int variables.

quiz.q: Sum is too small. Why is it safe to move left (and never look at numbers[left] again)?
options: Even with the biggest number still in range it's too small, so numbers[left] can't pair with anything left
Because left is smaller than right
Because the answer is always in the middle
It isn't safe, it can skip the answer
To skip the pair already checked
Because left and right moved after the check

quiz.q: Why not reuse the hash map from Two Sum I?
options: It uses O(n) extra space, and this problem asks for O(1)
It gives wrong answers on sorted input

quiz.q: What's the most comparisons two pointers can make on n numbers?
options: n − 1: each comparison rules out one number
